content: Dizziness is not a standalone condition but rather a symptom that encompasses a broad range of subjective experiences. It is characterized by sensations of postural instability or illusory motion. This symptom is particularly common in individuals aged 65 and older, accounting for approximately 5% of primary care visits in this demographic. The term dizziness is nonspecific and is often used to describe various sensations, including vertigo, spinning, disequilibrium, giddiness, presyncope, faintness, lightheadedness, or a feeling of being woozy. It is one of the most frequently reported symptoms encountered by emergency physicians, primary care providers, neurologists, and otolaryngologists. Dizziness can be classified into four main subtypes based on the patient’s symptoms, including vertigo, presyncope, and disequilibrium. The underlying pathophysiology of dizziness depends on its etiology, which may include conditions such as orthostatic hypotension, benign paroxysmal positional vertigo (BPPV), Meniere’s disease, Parkinson’s disease, hyperventilation syndrome, peripheral neuropathy, and vestibular migraine. The causes of dizziness are diverse and may include hypotension, dehydration, arrhythmias, labyrinthitis, Meniere’s disease, stroke, or hypoglycemia. Additional causes can be linked to specific organ systems, such as cardiovascular, neurological, musculoskeletal, dermatological, endocrine, infectious, or pulmonary systems, as well as side effects of medications. It is essential to differentiate dizziness from other conditions that may present with similar symptoms, such as vertigo, nystagmus, and hearing problems. Differential diagnoses include vestibular neuritis, herpes simplex virus (HSV) oticus, Meniere’s disease, labyrinthine concussion, perilymphatic fistula, semicircular canal dehiscence syndrome, vestibular paroxysmia, Cogan syndrome, vestibular schwannoma, otitis media, aminoglycoside toxicity, recurrent vestibulopathy, vestibular migraine, epileptic vertigo, multiple sclerosis, brain tumors, cerebellar infarction or hemorrhage, brainstem ischemia, presyncope, and disequilibrium. Dizziness is one of the most common complaints in ambulatory care, accounting for nearly 8 million outpatient visits annually in the United States. Approximately 3 million patients in the U.S. experience dizziness, with a lifetime prevalence estimated at 30%. Idiopathic dizziness is frequently observed in individuals aged 25 years and older, particularly in emergency department settings. Several risk factors contribute to the development of dizziness. These include a family history of thromboembolic conditions (such as diabetes, hypertension, hypercholesterolemia, and rheumatic disease), cardiac arrhythmias, stroke, and medication side effects. Medications associated with dizziness include diuretics, antiepileptic drugs, opioid-based analgesics, antipsychotics, antidepressants, antihypertensives, antifungals, lithium, benzodiazepines, antiarrhythmics, antimalarials, and anti-HIV drugs. Other risk factors include multiple sclerosis, seizures, brain tumors, benign positional vertigo, and labyrinthitis. If left untreated, dizziness may resolve spontaneously in some cases. However, common complications include nausea, vomiting, fainting, falls, imbalance, hearing loss, and neurological issues. Specific maneuvers, such as the Dix-Hallpike or Epley maneuvers, may also lead to complications in some patients.
